UrzaLLM: mapping Urza's ideas

Urza's articles, video descriptions and two books, embedded with a multilingual language model, to see what he writes about, how his ideas connect, and how much of politics in general he covers.

956 / 978 / 976articles / videos / book paragraphs

All texts are shown in English translation; every computation uses the Czech originals. Use the menu or the ← → keys to move between sections. Interactive maps: hover for details, the switches swap variants.

Data and chunking

2,910chunks per language
956 / 978 / 976article / video / book chunks
0chunks where Czech and English don't line up

From raw data to chunks

  1. Articles and videos without duplicates. Of the 1,953 posts on Urza's blog, 997 only announce a video and have no text of their own; they would duplicate the video, which is represented by its own description, so they are left out. Kept are the 956 posts with text (171 of them link a video but add their own text). All 978 videos of the YouTube channel are included.
  2. Books cleaned. Both books, Anarchokapitalismus and Anarchoagorismus, were parsed into sections; their front matter was removed: about the book, about the author, dedication, acknowledgements and contents (935 + 954 words). Prefaces, epilogues and the appendices are content and stay.
  3. Video descriptions cleaned. 102 recurring lines (donation requests, crypto addresses, bank details, Urza's signature, separators) were removed from every description: 34% of all video words. Guest introductions stay, since they say who the video is with.
  4. Translated. Every item also exists in English, item by item, section by section.

Final chunking

SourceOne chunk isChunksMedian wordsLongest
Articlesthe whole article text956146621
Videosthe whole (cleaned) description97888717
Booksone paragraph976101345

Each chunk has the same ID in Czech and English (for example art-0000, vid-0544, AC-033-009 = book, section, paragraph). Every chunk fits easily within what the model reads at once (about 8,000 tokens), so nothing is split further or truncated. Word counts are Czech.

How long the chunks are

How to read it: share of each source's chunks by number of words. What it shows: articles (median 146 words) and video descriptions (median 88) range from a hashtag to several hundred words; book paragraphs are shorter and more even (median 101). The shortest book chunks are lines of dialogue in the opening stories and headings.

Articles and videos over time

How to read it: article (blue) and video (green) chunks per year; one chunk is one article or one video. What it shows: Urza's output moves from writing to video over the years; the books have no year here.

Czech and English

An English chunk has a median of 1.21 × the words of its Czech original (90% between 1.07 and 1.35), as expected for a translation; 9 chunks are identical in both languages (names, links, texts written in English). Only the Czech chunks are embedded; the presentation shows each chunk's English twin, found by its ID.

Raw vs source-centred maps

Does the embedding place Urza's texts by topic, or by kind of text (book prose, blog post, video description)? A coverage map needs the first.

What was done

  1. Three embedding variants of every chunk: with source (a context line in front naming the source, e.g. “Kniha Anarchokapitalismus › 10. Zdravotnictví”, “Článek „…“ (2017)”), no source (the same line without the word naming the source) and text only (nothing in front).
  2. Source-centring: for each source, the average of its vectors is subtracted from each of them. What all books (or all videos) share, such as style, length and context line, is removed; what makes one chunk differ from another, its topic, stays.
  3. Maps: both versions reduced to 2D with UMAP, which keeps neighbours together; the right map is rotated to line up with the left. Only who sits next to whom is meaningful, not distances between far clusters.
  4. Measure: how often a chunk's 10 nearest neighbours come from the same source.

The maps: raw (left) and source-centred (right)

Embedding variant

How to read it: each dot is one chunk, coloured by source (blue articles, orange books, green videos). Hover a dot to see the chunk; it is circled on the other map too. The boxes hide sources, the search highlights titles (try drug, school or bitcoin). The switch swaps the embedding variant.

Does centring help?

VariantArticlesBooksVideos
With source77% → 73%95% → 89%86% → 70%
No source74% → 73%94% → 89%80% → 70%
Text only69% → 71%80% → 76%74% → 67%

How to read it: share of a chunk's 10 nearest neighbours (full 1,024-dim vectors) that come from its own source, raw → source-centred. Lower means sources mix more.

Conclusions

  • Centring reduces grouping by source, most where the source is most visible. Videos drop by 16 points with the source line, 10 without the source word and 7 on text alone; books by 6, 5 and 5. Articles change little (+2 to -4 points): they already sit in the middle of the corpus.
  • The context line is the biggest source signal. Book chunks have 95% book neighbours with the line naming the source, and 80% on text alone. Text only is the honest basis for the maps.
  • What remains is genuine. After centring and without any context line, 67%–76% of neighbours still share the source: the books, the blog and the videos really do discuss partly different subjects. Inside the books, chunks group by chapter on content alone (48% same-chapter neighbours against 5% by chance): regions of the map correspond to ideas.

Linear structure: PCA and ICA

All 2,910 chunks (text-only embeddings) projected onto straight axes. Unlike UMAP, every axis is one fixed direction in the 1,024-dimensional space, so it can be read and measured.

What was done

  1. Centring: the average vector of all chunks is subtracted (one average for all, not per source).
  2. PCA finds the directions of largest variation, in order; ICA (20 components) finds directions whose scores are as independent and long-tailed as possible, so each tends to pick out one theme or one kind of text.
  3. Reading an axis: the chunks at its two ends, their mix of sources, the video tags and book chapters over-represented among them. η² = share of an axis' variance explained by the source alone (0 = none, 1 = the axis only tells articles, books and videos apart).

How much does each direction explain?

How to read it: share of all variation captured by each of the first 20 principal components. PC1 explains 6.3%; no direction dominates.

How to read it: variance explained by the first k components together. Half the variation needs 52 components, 90% needs 270: the meaning of the texts is spread over many directions, so no flat map can show all of it.

How to read it: 8 of the 20 components are themes (their 30 top chunks come from several sources), 12 are formats or series (at least 80% from one source: a recurring kind of post, a video series, or one book chapter); the five most focused of each are shown. Kurtosis measures how long-tailed a component's scores are: a high value means a few chunks score extremely high and the rest near zero, so the component is sharply focused on one subject; a low value means it is spread over many texts.

ICA map

How to read it: chunks placed by two ICA components (selectable). Because themes cut across sources, colours mix far more here than on the PCA map.

Conclusions

  • No dominant direction: PC1 covers 6.3%, and half the variation needs 52 components.
  • Is the strongest direction really the kind of text? Only because this PCA keeps the differences between sources. Here only one overall average was removed, so the gap between the average article, book and video stays in the data: 4% of all variation, and PC1 picks it up (η² 0.36). Checked separately: with each source's own average removed, as for the maps, PC1 explains 5% and no axis separates the sources any more (η² 0.00). The “kind of text” is a shift between sources, not a structure within the topics.
  • Beneath it, the axes are topics: from PC2 on the source explains little, and ICA finds 8 themes shared by books, articles and videos (crypto, the Austrian school, the book campaign, drugs, …).
  • The rest are formats: 12 ICA components each capture one recurring kind of post, series or book chapter, useful to spot template texts.

The book idea map

Do regions of the map correspond to ideas? The books are the cleanest test: their chapters are topic labels written by the author.

What was done

  1. Data: the 976 book paragraphs with their embeddings, in two variants: with the chapter path in front of each chunk (no source: “Anarchokapitalismus › 10. Zdravotnictví”) and from the text alone (text only).
  2. Chapter groups: each paragraph belongs to one of 56 groups: a chapter, or for the appendix of Anarchokapitalismus its topic or AMEN category; the aphorisms form one group.
  3. Maps: UMAP and, as a check, t-SNE, on the book chunks only; each chapter's name sits at the average position of its chunks. A far-away island (the opening stories) is moved closer for display; measurements use the original layout.
  4. Measures: who are each chunk's 10 nearest neighbours, and how tightly each chapter sits on the map (its spread relative to a random set of the same size: 1 = random, below 0.2 = compact).

UMAP and t-SNE maps

Embedding variant

How to read it: each dot is a paragraph, coloured by book (blue Anarchokapitalismus, orange Anarchoagorismus). Click a chapter in the list, or on the map, to highlight it on both maps; hover for the text. The switch swaps the variant.

How tight is each chapter?

How to read it: each dot is one chapter group (colour = book), placed by its spread relative to a random set (log scale; left = tighter); the vertical mark is the median. Hover a dot for the chapter. What it shows: with the chapter path in front, almost every chapter is a tight island (median 0.04); on text alone chapters spread more (median 0.17) but most are still far tighter than random. t-SNE spreads everything a little more, keeping the same order.

Conclusions

  • Chapters are ideas on the map. On text alone, 48% of a paragraph's nearest neighbours are from its own chapter, against 5% by chance, and 35 of 56 chapters form compact regions.
  • The chapter label inflates this: with the path in front, same-chapter neighbours rise to 73% and 49 chapters are compact; the label accounts for about 37% of the above-chance grouping. The text-only map is the honest one.
  • Not an artefact of UMAP: t-SNE agrees on which chapters are compact and which are spread out (rank correlation 0.92 on text only, 0.82 with the path).
  • Related chapters are neighbours, also across the two books: the two education chapters sit together, and the AMEN objections on economics next to the chapter on central planning they answer.

Trails between book topics

On the book map, sections sit next to related sections; following those neighbours reads like a line of argument. Here the neighbourhoods become a network of links between the 65 book sections.

What was done

  1. Links from the text: for every book paragraph (text-only embedding), its 10 most similar paragraphs are taken; each neighbour from a different section counts as one link between the two sections.
  2. Lift measures how strong a link is: the number of links between two sections divided by the number expected if neighbours were picked at random. Big sections would collect many links just by size; lift corrects for that. Lift 1 = chance, lift 10 = ten times more often than chance. Kept are links with lift ≥ 2 and at least 3 neighbour pairs: 237 links.
  3. Paths: between two sections, the chain of strongest links (each step costs 1 / lift); for every step the most similar pair of passages across it is shown, the actual bridge between the topics.

The trail map

How to read it: circles are sections (size = number of paragraphs, colour = book), lines are links (thicker = higher lift). Pick two sections, or a suggested pair, to see the trail between them and the passages that bridge each step.

The backbone

The backbone is the maximum spanning tree of the network: the 63 strongest links that still connect every section, without loops. It removes redundant links and keeps the main lines of argument, so it is the skeleton the trails follow; 13 of its links join the two books, the places where both books discuss the same thing. Conclusions

  • The topics form connected trails that follow the books' arguments, for example 2. Education → 3. Indoctrination → 9. Democracy, or Drugs → smugglers and dealers → Liberation Travel → 22. Love.
  • Broad sections are hubs: Myth busting, 8. State, 20. Participation, 21. The future connect the most topics.
  • Only the opening stories stand apart: as narrative dialogue, they have no strong link to any section.

Topic distribution

The books are Urza's most systematic statement. Here they define the concepts, and the articles and videos are sorted into them: which of his book topics does he return to?

What was done

  1. Concept space from the books: PCA on the book paragraphs only, keeping the directions that carry more than a random split would; each source's average is removed first so style doesn't decide.
  2. Concept centres: the average of each book section's paragraphs. Every article and video chunk is assigned to the most similar centre (announcements left out).
68%of book paragraphs land back in their own section when taken out and re-assigned (chance 1.5%): the sections are distinct enough to sort texts into.
58 / 58topical book sections that at least some articles or videos are sorted into: no book topic is left untouched.
0.26 / 0.25median similarity of articles / videos to their section centre, against 0.42 for the books' own paragraphs: they fit the book topics, but more loosely, since they also discuss current events the books don't.

Distribution over the books' concepts

How to read it: each bar is a book section: the share of article and video chunks assigned to it, compared with the section's share of the books. Hover for example texts.

Conclusions

  • Every book topic recurs, most of all Free port, Cryptocurrency, Hedgehog without a cage.
  • The two books split the output: articles lean to Anarchokapitalismus topics (61%), videos to Anarchoagorismus (56%), in line with the shift over time towards the second book's themes.
  • The broad picture is robust; the exact ranking is not: it changes with the size of the concept space.

Urza in the political space

Everything so far measured Urza against himself. Here the reference is independent of him: a map of politics in general, and how much of it he addresses.

54%of questions with a strongly matching Urza passage (≥ 0.60)
93%of questions with at least a relevant passage (≥ 0.55)
85 / 85subtopics that some of his texts are closest to

By volume he writes most about Government and public administration, Law and justice, Education; his answers are least direct in Energy, European Union and international relations, Environment.

What was done

  • The political space: 326 items built on the Comparative Agendas Project classification: 22 policy areas, their subtopics, concrete questions as Czech voters meet them, and concepts of political philosophy.
  • Same model as Urza's texts (bge-m3); topics and concepts embedded as “name: description”, questions as written.
  • Depth of an item: the similarity of Urza's single best-matching passage, as a search would rank it (≥ 0.55 relevant, ≥ 0.60 squarely on topic).
  • Volume of an area: how many of his chunks are closest to its subtopics (each source's average removed first; announcements left out).
  • Map: the political items laid out with UMAP (each item type's average removed so items group by subject, not wording); Urza's chunks are then added without changing it, in three ways (switch above the map).

The map of the political space

How to read it: large dots are subtopics, small dots questions, squares concepts; colour = depth of Urza's best passage (darker = covered more squarely). Small dots behind are Urza's chunks. Hover an item for its best passage; the placement switch changes how his chunks are placed, not the political map.
